note: The title tells you straight: this is Solomon's song, the wisest king of Israel singing about love. He could've written a thousand treatises, but what he leaves us is a poem—because some truths only poetry can hold.

She opens her heart with longing: his kisses are worth more than wine. I've seen older loves still remember this ache—that moment when you want someone so much the world goes quiet. The Spirit knows this yearning too, and He meets it.

His reputation spreads like fragrant oil poured out—you can't contain it, it fills a room, draws people in. This is what love does when it's genuine: it becomes visible, felt, wanted by many. The young women love him because he is good.

She wants to run with him, enter his chambers, be safe with him, celebrate him out loud. Notice she doesn't say 'I wish'—she says 'we will rejoice.' Even in longing, she speaks as if belonging. That's the voice of faith making itself felt.

She names herself 'dark, but lovely'—not dark instead of lovely, but dark AND lovely. A woman who's known hardship, sun-scorched by labor, yet she holds her worth without apology. This is courage: to see yourself truthfully and still say, I belong here.

She was set to tend vineyards—her mother's sons made her keeper while they looked after their own. Yet in a single look from him, the work-worn hands become precious. He doesn't see only what the world made her do; he sees her.

She asks: where do you rest at noon? She's looking for him in the rhythms of his day—wanting to know the ordinary moments, not just the romance. Real love asks this: how do you spend your hours? Where do you belong?

He doesn't give directions; he tells her: follow the sheep, graze your goats with the shepherds. It's a gentle riddle: if you truly seek me, you'll find me doing what I do—leading, caring, being faithful. Come join that life.

A steed in Pharaoh's chariot—a creature of beauty and strength, harnessed but not broken. He sees her power, her grace, her readiness. Not fragile or decorative; vital, purposeful, at home in high places.

He marks the beauty she already has—her cheeks, her neck adorned—but he's not flattering her; he's seeing what was there. Admiration that notices the real person is a gift, especially for someone the world has taught to hide.

We will make you gold earrings with silver studs. He's not alone in this—his household, his companions join in. Love isn't private; it celebrates and honors in view of others. She becomes adorned not as his possession but as valued by everyone near him.

While the king sits at his table, her perfume fills the air—she's present in his moment, her presence is known, appreciated. She didn't speak, but she was there, and it mattered. Sometimes just being known is enough.

Myrrh was bitter, used in death rites and healing—she says he is this to her, lying close to her heart. Real love holds both fragrance and sting, both comfort and cost. She's not looking for easy; she's looking for true.

En Gedi's vineyards were famed, remote, precious—she places him in abundance and beauty, a real place made sacred by memory. When you love truly, ordinary places become gardens, and his presence is the harvest.

He repeats it twice: you are beautiful, you are beautiful—as if once wasn't enough to convince her. Her eyes are doves: gentle, watchful, innocent. He is saying: I know you, and you are worth repeating.

Our couch is verdant—green, living, growing. Even in intimate language, they speak of what is alive and fruitful, not fading. Love that stays young is love rooted in something steady, something that keeps giving life back.

Cedars and firs—strong wood, fragrant, built to last. Readers today hear an echo here: a house built on the best materials, on faithfulness. In a world of cheap things, they chose to build with what endures. Looking back from a longer road, I see now that's where real love makes its home.

She calls herself a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys—flowers that grow wild, uncultivated, in common places. This is the beloved speaking, yet she names herself in humility, not grandeur. There's a lesson here about how the Lord sees us, not by our striving, but as flowers He has made to grow in the very ground where we stand.

Her beloved answers: among all the daughters, she stands out like a lily among thorns. When someone truly loves us, they see us that way—not comparing us to a standard, but recognizing something precious in us that they treasure above all else. This is how Christ sees His own.

She draws another image: as an apple tree stands out among common forest wood, so does her beloved among the sons. Now she sits beneath his shadow, and his fruit is sweet to her taste—an intimate rest and a found provision. This is the language of protection and nourishment intertwined.

He has brought her to the banquet hall—a place of gathering and gladness. His banner over her is love: not a banner of conquest, but of belonging. In ancient custom, a banner marked a household's protection and claim. Here it speaks of being marked and sealed by love itself.

She is faint with love and asks to be strengthened with raisins and refreshed with apples—small gifts, simple comfort. There's honesty here: love can overwhelm us, leave us weak-kneed and needing to be held up. Yet she asks, and in asking, shows that she trusts him to understand.

His left hand under her head, his right hand holding her close—an embrace that's both cradling and encompassing. In Scripture, the right hand often speaks of strength and favor. Here both hands are at work: one offering rest, the other offering security.

She speaks to the daughters of Jerusalem: do not awaken love before its time. This is wisdom learned from watching others. Love, when it truly comes, is not forced or rushed—it arrives as it will. There's a patience here that speaks to something deeper than mere passion.

His voice! She recognizes it from far away—leaping on the mountains, skipping the hills like a young buck in his joy. She hears before she sees, and the sound of him transforms the landscape itself into a place of motion and life.

He stands beyond the wall, looking through windows and lattice—not yet inside, but present, seeking her. There's a tenderness to this watching; he peers in, not commanding entry but longing to see her. The barrier between them only makes his eagerness more apparent.

He speaks: 'Rise up, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.' These are words of invitation, not demand. He calls her both by her relation to him ('my love') and by her worth ('my beautiful one'). He bids her to rise and join him in motion, in freedom.

Winter is past, rain is over and gone—the invitation carries the weight of a season turned. All that was cold and drowning has passed. Now is the time to emerge, to move, to begin again. The invitation is not only to him, but to a new season itself.

Flowers appear on the earth, turtledoves sing—the signs of spring are specific and sensory. In Middle Eastern custom, the turtledove's call marked the turning season and the renewal of love songs. She hears the world itself calling her forth into this moment.

Fig trees bear green figs, vines blossom and exhale fragrance—the natural world is alive and fertile, heavy with promise. Into this abundance he calls her again: 'Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.' All of creation seems to echo his invitation.

He calls her his dove in the clefts of the rock—a creature hiding, safe in rocky places. Yet he asks to see her face and hear her voice, to know her completely. There's no hiding from love that truly sees us; he wants not just her safety, but her full presence.

Catch the little foxes that plunder the vineyards—while the vines are tender and in blossom. These small destroyers come when the harvest is most vulnerable. It's a word of caution: tend carefully to what you are building, for small neglects can ruin what blooms.

My beloved is mine, and I am his; he browses among the lilies. She claims him fully, and he claims her; they belong to one another. The image of him among lilies brings us back to where we began—to flowers and gardens, to a place where love takes root and grows naturally.

Until the day is cool and shadows flee away, turn and be swift as a roe on the mountains. Readers today hear an echo in this urgency: love asks for our presence while we are present, for the day grows shorter than we realize. Come away now, not in some distant morning.
Night searching—the lover's restlessness speaks of yearning so keen it cannot wait for daylight. The search that fails is not wasted; it's the deepest confession of desire the soul can make.
Rising from bed, she walks the dark city streets calling out. There's a urgency here that passes beyond propriety—she is undone by longing, and she doesn't hide it. That's love unguarded.
The night watchmen meet her search. Even strangers witness the beloved's desperation. Sometimes our hunger for the good reveals itself to those we don't expect—and that's all right.
After the dark wandering, she finds him—and holds. The rush to bring him to her mother's house speaks of joy that claims him publicly, that won't let go. Finding is only half; holding is the rest.
She charges Jerusalem's daughters—let love awaken in its own time. There's a restraint here, a wisdom: you cannot hurry the heart's ripe season. Even desire has its proper moment.

The caravan rises from the wilderness—myrrh and frankincense were costly trade goods from southern lands, symbols of wealth and reverence. This approaching figure comes perfumed like a king bringing gifts of honor.
Solomon's carriage is surrounded by sixty warriors—a royal procession. The lover recognizes the grandeur of his approach. To be chosen by one of such dignity is to be raised to his station.
Each warrior skilled in battle, sword at hand—yet here they serve not war but the protection of love. Even might bends to tenderness when it guards what is precious.
The carriage itself is wrought with care—Lebanon's finest wood. To offer a beloved something you have labored to make beautiful is a language all its own.
Silver pillars, gold base, purple seat—and all paved 'with love' from Jerusalem's daughters. The carriage itself is an offering of affection. Every detail speaks devotion.

Come see the king crowned by his mother, on his wedding day—readers today hear an echo of the Bridegroom crowned by His people, the Church made radiant as His beloved. Every true wedding points beyond itself to that final covenant.

When love speaks, it starts with seeing—really seeing—the beloved as wholly beautiful. Those eyes like doves recall something tender and watchful. Mount Gilead was a place of healing balm, and I think that's the longing here: to see someone with the tenderness of one who knows all the hurt they've carried and loves them still.

The image of teeth like a newly shorn flock speaks to an ancient custom of preparing wool—cleaned, matched, complete. In the beloved's presence, he sees not just beauty but wholeness and care: nothing missing, nothing bereaved. That's how love counts: in the quiet joy of finding someone entire.

Scarlet thread was a sign of worth in Scripture—drawn across Rahab's window, marking her for redemption. Lips that speak, temples that frame her face—the admirer is seeing not just surface but the places where her person shows itself to the world.

David's tower was not mere ornament; it held shields—protection and strength. To see a beloved's neck as such a tower is to recognize that their beauty carries dignity and steadiness. The mighty men hang their shields there in trust. What a thing to tell someone: you are someone I can rest against.

Twin fawns feeding among lilies—the image holds both gentleness and freedom. The beloved is not ornament but alive, moving, nourishing herself in beauty. The admirer watches and delights not in possession but in the grace of her living.

This is desire spoken as pilgrimage: the day turning cool, shadows shortening, and the lover willing to journey toward myrrh and frankincense—the fragrant, precious places. It's not hasty appetite but a journey of devotion, each step carrying him nearer to what matters most.

No spot, no blemish—the beloved is whole to him, not because she has no struggles but because in the presence of true love, we are seen for what we are beneath the hurt and shadow. Christ speaks this way to His bride: spotless, not through our own cleansing but through His eyes of love.

Lebanon, Amana, Senir, Hermon—mountains named with meaning. He calls her to leave the high places, those peaks where lions and leopards prowl, and come down with him. It's a call from danger into trust, from solitude into companionship, from the wild heights into his kept presence.

Ravished—a strong word, and it means captured completely. One eye, one chain of gold at the neck: not by assault but by the small, simple signs of her presence. A single glance, a single token. This is how love works—not through grand theater but through the exact particular of one beloved.

Wine and perfume—the good things of life lose their savor when set beside the beloved. Her love surpasses all that once seemed beautiful because it comes from her, specific and known and freely given. In Christ, we taste this too: that knowing Him makes all other glory shadows.

Honey and milk under her tongue—what she speaks is sweet and nourishing. The fragrance of her garments carries the scent of Lebanon, that place of cedars and height and noble beauty. To be near her is to be near something that feeds and that lifts the spirit.

A locked garden, a sealed fountain—not locked against him who calls her beloved, but locked against the careless or the false. Her depths are kept, precious, offered only to the one who comes with genuine love. There is mystery here, and safety in mystery; not all of us should have all of each other.

Pomegranates, henna, spikenard—every plant here was costly and precious, grown with care. Spikenard especially marked the woman who anointed Jesus' feet, pouring out wealth in worship. The beloved is not ornamental but a garden of worth, each growth placed with intention.

Saffron, calamus, cinnamon, myrrh, aloes—the spices that were brought to the newborn Christ, that anointed the dead, that marked the holy. In his beloved he perceives not common beauty but something bearing the weight of the sacred, of worship, of remembrance.

A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters flowing from Lebanon—she is not still but alive, flowing, generative. What she holds is not stagnant but moves and nourishes all it touches. In this image, the beloved is the source of life itself to him, the one from whom all good flows.

Readers today hear an echo in this: the awakening of all winds, north and south, called to stir the garden so its fragrance rises—a picture of a life fully alive, fragrant, open to wind and sky. When we give ourselves wholly to Christ, we too become a garden where all the winds of His Spirit blow, and something precious rises up that the whole world catches the scent of.

The beloved enters the beloved's garden—a place of belonging, gathered fruit, and satisfaction. The Lord invites His friends, His beloved ones, to eat and drink abundantly. There is nothing stingy about His love; He spreads a feast and bids us come near.

She sleeps, yet her heart watches—that tender state we know when love keeps us half-awake. He stands at the door, dew-soaked from the night's journey, calling out. How often the Lord knocks when we are drowsy, asking us to open, to be present to His presence.

Her resistance is plain: she has settled in, why trouble herself? She hesitates. We do the same, don't we—finding comfort in our own arrangements, reluctant to rise and answer when love calls. Yet love waits at the threshold.

His hand reaches through the latch—a sign of intimacy, a threshold crossed. Her heart awakens at his touch, no longer drowsy or unmoved. The gesture is tender and urgent at once: he is here, he is reaching for her, and her whole self stirs to life.

Now she moves—her hands stained with myrrh as she unfastens the lock, anointed as though for a wedding. The fragrance clings to her as she rises to let him in. Precious things mark the moment; she is made fragrant by her own readiness.

She opens the door, but he is gone. Her beloved has departed, leaving her heart behind with his words but his presence nowhere to be found. The taste of loss is bitter when love has called us awake only to vanish. She searches, calls, but hears nothing in return.

The city's watchmen find her—not as a protector, but as an obstacle. They strike her, strip her of her cloak. In her search for her beloved through the dark streets, she is treated as an intruder. We know this kind of grief: the world shows no mercy to those who are lovesick and lost.

She calls to the daughters of Jerusalem, adjuring them to carry her message if they find her beloved: tell him I am faint with love. She has nothing left but her longing, no shield, no dignity—only the ache of love that has grown unbearable. She stakes everything on the hope that someone will listen.

They ask her back: what makes your beloved different? Why should we care? The question cuts—she has been beaten, stripped, and now her passion is questioned. Yet it drives her to speak: let me tell you. The beloved is worth everything she has suffered in searching.

He is white and ruddy—color and life, wholeness and vigor. He stands out among ten thousand; there is no one like him. She begins her portrait with those words that say: he is unmistakable, radiant, one of a kind. Love speaks in superlatives because it sees truly.

His head like purest gold, his hair dark and full—she paints him in precious metals and deep colors. There is majesty in the image: crowned, strong, not a wisp but substantial. She describes him as though building a shrine word by word.

Eyes like doves beside the water—soft, watching, alive with clarity. Washed with milk, set like jewels: pure and precious, catching light. How a bride describes the eyes of her beloved! She sees kindness and attentiveness, beauty and worth, all in the gaze turned toward her.

His cheeks like a garden of spices, his lips like lilies dripping myrrh. She moves from the noble to the tender—the softness of his face, the sweetness of his words. He is fragrant, alive with flavor; to be near him is to be near abundance and delight.

His hands like gold rings set with beryl, his body like ivory overlaid with sapphires. She continues the portrait of beauty joined to strength—not ornament alone, but craftsmanship and value. Every part speaks of care, design, and precious worth.

His legs like marble pillars on gold sockets, his presence like Lebanon's excellence. She describes stability, foundation, majesty. He does not sway or diminish. His very bearing echoes the grandeur of the cedars—ancient, rooted, enduring.

His mouth is sweetness; he is altogether lovely. She names him her beloved and her friend—both at once. Readers today hear an echo in those words: the Jesus of the Gospels, who calls Himself the Bridegroom and invites us as His friends, altogether lovely and altogether worthy. She has spoken her beloved into being.
How gently the friends ask where her beloved has gone—not blaming, but inviting themselves into the search. It's the way love makes us want to help someone find what they've lost, what they ache for.
She knows exactly where he is—his garden, his work, his place. Beloved and beloved know each other's haunts, their rhythms. There's comfort in that knowing.
Notice the beautiful clarity: *I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine.* This is covenant speech—belonging sealed both ways. The lilies bloom where he is; she dwells in his gaze.

Tirzah and Jerusalem—real cities, real beauty—yet she surpasses them both. Awesome as an army with banners: she radiates strength, dignity, joy that turns heads. The beloved sees not flattery but truth in her.
His plea—*turn away your eyes*—shows how her gaze undoes him, overcomes his composure. Then he praises her hair like goats on Gilead's slopes. In love, even a teasing restraint is tender.
Teeth like ewes fresh-washed, each bearing twins, none bereaved—a picture of wholeness, vitality, care. He sees her not as an object but as alive, flourishing, complete.
A pomegranate glimpsed behind the veil—mystery and beauty held together. He honors what is revealed and what is veiled, what is public and what is her own.
The court teems with beauty—queens, concubines, unnumbered virgins—yet his heart has chosen one. Abundance surrounds him; she alone moves him. That's not blindness; that's love.

His dove, his perfect one, unique—her mother's darling, chosen above all. Even the daughters and queens acclaim her. He doesn't diminish others to lift her up; her worth speaks for itself, recognized by those who see her.
Who is she? The question hangs—she arrives like the morning itself, beautiful as the moon, clear as the sun. She is her own mystery even to those who long for her.
He descends into the garden to see what grows, what promises to bud—vines, pomegranates. Gardens are places of tending, of hope. His soul seeks what is alive and becoming.

Without realizing it, desire has set him among the royal chariots. Love carries us into places we didn't plan to go, makes us part of processions we didn't foresee. We wake surprised to find ourselves already chosen.

Return, return—the word echoes three times. Readers today hear an echo of that same gentle, urgent longing: turn back, come home, let yourself be beheld. The Shulammite, perfected and unique, dances not to escape but to be seen and loved.

The lover's gaze moves from feet upward, and even the smallest detail—sandals, thighs—becomes a language of praise. What strikes me is how presence itself is the gift: to be seen fully and honored wholly. The workmanship of a skilled hand speaks to how God has made each beloved with intention.

Wine unmixed, wheat gathered, lilies blooming—the beloved's body is described as abundance and fruitfulness. I've learned that desire itself, when held within covenant, can point to something holy: the way God provides, the way He satisfies, the way abundance is meant to be shared and received.
Fawns—tender, graceful, alive. In covenant love, our bodies are not shameful; they are meant to be delighted in by one another. The Lord who made us has not taken back what He made; He calls it good.

Heshbon, Bathrabbim, Lebanon, Damascus—this is the landscape of the beloved's beauty, mapped onto real places. I see in this the lover saying: *You are as vast and real and particular to me as these cities are.* Love doesn't generalize; it names and remembers.

Carmel rises over the plain; the head crowned with hair like purple silk—regal, captivating. The king held captive in her tresses: in covenant love, we surrender to one another willingly. That yielding, not losing oneself, is where freedom and delight meet.

After the careful, intricate praise comes this simple word: *Beautiful. Pleasant.* Sometimes the deepest compliment is the unadorned one—a beloved simply seen and simply loved for the sake of love itself, not for performance or proving.

A palm tree: tall, fruitful, stable, noble. The stature of the beloved speaks to character as much as form. When we love well, we see both the body and the soul it carries—the height of who they are becoming in Christ.

To climb, to gather, to enjoy the fruit—the language is active, generous, and shared. The shift to apples and vines reminds us that covenant love is not static; it's alive, growing, seasoned by the beloved's presence itself. Each meeting is a harvest.

Wine, best wine, wine that flows and glides—there is intoxication in love, a rightful losing of oneself in another's presence. The beloved's mouth is not a thing to be taken; it is a gift that dissolves into communion, like wine shared in peace.

Three clauses, two voices: *I am his. His desire is toward me.* Belonging and being desired—not opposed, but one truth told two ways. In Christ's love for His bride, we see both the security of ownership and the joy of being pursued. Both are grace.

The invitation shifts outward: come, let us go to the field, lodge in villages. Love does not hide in a chamber alone; it moves out into the world, witnessed, lived, generous with itself. The beloved calls the lover to adventure together.

Early to the vineyards, watching for first blossoms, pomegranates in flower—the season of anticipation. And then: *There I will give you my love.* The gift is not hurried; it is timed to the opening of creation itself. Desire, rightly ordered, waits for the moment to ripen.

Mandrakes, precious fruits, new and old—a treasury stored up. Readers today hear an echo in this: the beloved who has saved love, who speaks of what has been gathered over time. We are moved when someone says *I have kept this for you,* aren't we? That's how the Lord speaks to those He loves. He has saved all His gifts for us.

She longs for a love that is public and safe, not hidden and fraught with shame. This ache—to love freely without fear of judgment—runs deep in the human heart. The Gospel whispers that in Christ we are already loved out in the open, nothing to hide.

She envisions bringing her beloved into the sanctuary of home and mother's wisdom, sharing wine and fruit—the intimate furnishings of a life built together. There is tenderness here in the notion that love finds its fullness when it settles into family and belonging.

Left hand beneath the head, right arm embracing—she rests in his strength and protection, held from both sides. This is the mutuality Solomon's song keeps turning back to: a beloved who carries and is carried.

For the third time, the beloved adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love until it desires (see 2:7, 3:5). The refrain anchors the song's pulse: love is not forced or hurried, but draws us forward in its own season. Even in joy, there is patience.

The scene at the apple tree—where the young man awakened his beloved, where her mother once conceived and labored to bring him forth—collapses time and return. Places hold memory; love walks ground that has known both beginning and bearing.

Love as a seal stamped upon heart and arm—indelible, binding, as fierce as death itself. The song reaches its summit here: this love cannot be undone, and its intensity is likened to a flame of Yahweh, the very fire of God. Few verses capture so plainly love's sacred weight.

No flood drowns it, no wealth can purchase it. Love stands sovereign above every other treasure—it is worth all a man possesses and yet cannot be traded for. This verse strips away illusion: money cannot answer what the human heart truly craves.

Siblings speak of their little sister, not yet ready for marriage—a moment of tenderness and concern. They ask what they shall do for her, what protection or preparation she needs. It is a reminder that love and sexuality are not solitary but woven into kinship and care.

The brothers propose contingencies: if she is a wall (strong, resolute), they build upon her strength; if she is a door (more open, vulnerable), they close her with boards of cedar for protection. Either way, family stands ready to honor what she is and shield her from harm.

She replies: I am a wall, and my breasts like towers—a claim of her own solidity and readiness. Yet it was in his eyes that she found peace, not in her own virtue or strength alone. This is the paradox: we become whole when we are truly seen by one who loves us.

Solomon's vineyard at Baal Hamon—a place and a name anchor the comparison. Keepers bring a thousand shekels each for the vineyard's fruit. The song moves now from the secret garden to a royal estate, perhaps to signal the gap between common love and the world's measure of worth.

My own vineyard is before me, she says—not leased out or managed by keepers, but her own. The thousand goes to Solomon; two hundred to the tenders. She keeps her own garden, her own love, and gives what she will give. There is sovereignty in her choice.

He calls to her from the gardens where friends gather—an invitation to be heard, to break silence, to speak into the world where others dwell. Love that stays locked away grows small; love that finds its voice grows bold.

Come away, my beloved—the final word is movement, urgency, freedom. Readers today hear an echo in this: the call to step away from lesser things and follow love to heights we have not yet climbed. Jesus says, Come away with me too.
